source.title: CodeFuse-13B: A Pretrained Multi-Lingual Code Large Language Model
source.authors: Peng Di; Jian-Guo Li; Hang Yu; Wei Jiang; Wen-Ting Cai; Yang Cao; Chao-Yu Chen; Da-Jun Chen; Hongwei Chen; Liang Chen; Gang Fan; Jie Gong; Zi Gong; Wen Hu; Tingting Guo; Zhichao Lei; Ting Li; Zheng Li; Ming Liang; Cong Liao; Bingchang Liu; Jiachen Liu; Zhi-Wei Liu; Shaojun Lu; Mingquan Shen; Guangpei Wang; Huan Wang; Zhi Wang; Zhaogui Xu; Jia-Wei Yang; Qing Ye; Gehao Zhang; Yu Zhang; Zelin Zhao; Xunjin Zheng; Hailian Zhou; Lifu Zhu; Xianying Zhu

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports HumanEval pass@1 scores across several CodeFuse model sizes, bearing on downstream performance with scale, but it does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports HumanEval scores for four CodeFuse releases with stated sizes. The paper also discusses training/validation-loss monitoring but gives no loss results. Results for other models in Table 4 are attributed to published reports and are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: A model release report. Table 1 is a product roadmap: monthly releases in which size, sequence length, data iteration and fine-tuning stage change together. The authors credit the gains to 'monthly model iterations', not to scale. No loss curves, fits, or controlled size sweep are reported. Hoffmann et al. appears only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that CodeFuse-13B reaches 37.10% HumanEval pass@1, is among the top multilingual models of similar size, and outperforms others on Chinese-prompt code tasks. They draw no scaling-law conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Reports downstream HumanEval performance across a small family of code models; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit the original scaling-law relationships.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size changes alongside release date and sequence length in the early progression; the 13B base and September releases differ in fine-tuning stage.

fits_no_version.finding: Across internal releases (1.3B, 6.5B, 13B base, 13B fine-tuned), HumanEval pass@1 rises from 11.58% to 37.10%. Size, sequence length, data iteration and fine-tuning all change together.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Successive industrial code-LLM releases of increasing size show rising HumanEval scores, without isolating scale from data or recipe changes.

record.problems: The size progression is small, with no uncertainty reported or controls isolating size from sequence length, release, and training-stage differences. The results are benchmark scores, not a fitted or validated prediction.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; training/validation loss is only monitored, never reported.
Table 3 lists differing depth and width per size, but no fixed-size shape comparison.
Code-heavy pretraining, but no power-law fit.
No controlled relation between scale and downstream score; the 350M model has no reported score; no fits.
Nothing on fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Table 4 reports CodeFuse-13B-Base HumanEval Python pass@1 as 24.83%, contradicting Table 1's 32.93% for the same model.
missing.versions: none (V6 if the rows were kept)

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V6 'supports' label are dropped. The size progression is an uncontrolled product roadmap: the 13B gain in r4 comes from fine-tuning, and the base score is inconsistent between Tables 1 and 4. This study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No comparison of scaling laws across modalities or training regimes.
The reported size progression gives benchmark scores but does not test predictive fits, pretraining-loss relationships, or downstream performance beyond HumanEval.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curvature away from power laws.

rows.subject: CodeFuse-1.3B-2K Seq-Length
rows.operation_detail: Reported HumanEval pass@1 for a member of the CodeFuse model progression.
rows.note: One of four CodeFuse releases whose scores increase with the stated model-size progression.
rows.check: Roadmap entry, not a scaling manipulation. Size is confounded with release date, sequence length (2K vs 4K) and data iteration. No baseline.

rows.subject: CodeFuse-6.5B-4K Seq-Length
rows.operation_detail: Reported HumanEval pass@1 for a member of the CodeFuse model progression.
rows.note: The score is higher than the reported 1.3B release; sequence length also differs.
rows.check: Table 1 names this model 6.5B, but Table 3 lists the family member as 6B. It also differs from r1 in sequence length and release, so the size effect cannot be isolated.

rows.subject: CodeFuse-13B-Base-4K Seq-Length
rows.operation_detail: Reported HumanEval pass@1 for the base model in the CodeFuse progression.
rows.note: The score is higher than the earlier reported releases.
rows.check: Table 1 gives 32.93% HumanEval for the 13B base, but Table 4 gives CodeFuse-13B-Base 24.83% Python pass@1. The value is internally inconsistent. It is also confounded with release iteration.

rows.subject: CodeFuse-13B
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned by LoRA/QLoRA on multiple code tasks using the self-pretrained base model
rows.operation_detail: Reported HumanEval pass@1 for the September CodeFuse release.
rows.note: Same stated parameter count as the May base model, but this release is fine-tuned.
rows.check: Same 13B size as r3; the gain comes from LoRA/QLoRA multi-task fine-tuning, not scale. Table 1 dates it Jun 2023 (opened in Sep), not Sep. It should not count as a point in a size progression.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The four CodeFuse releases in Table 1
reader_labels.reason: Reported HumanEval scores rise from 11.58% to 37.10% across the listed releases, including increasing scores at 1.3B, 6.5B, and 13B; see r1–r4. This is not a test of predictive fits.
